name: Graph Representation (Adjacency List)
description: The most common way to represent a graph in JavaScript interviews. An adjacency list stores each node's neighbors in an object or Map, enabling O(1) neighbor access and O(V + E) traversal.

examples.title: Example 1: Build Adjacency List from Edge List
examples.explanation: Iterates edges once. For undirected graphs, add both directions. Time O(E), Space O(V + E). Use Map() if node values aren't strings or numbers.

examples.title: Example 2: Using Map() for Non-String Nodes
examples.explanation: Map() is preferred when nodes are objects, arrays, or non-primitive types. Same O(E) build time. Iteration uses graph.keys() and graph.get(node).

name: DFS (Depth First Search)
description: Explores as far down a branch as possible before backtracking. Implemented recursively or with an explicit stack. Used for path finding, cycle detection, connected components, and tree traversal.

examples.title: Example 1: Recursive DFS (Connected Components)
examples.explanation: Recursive DFS visits each node once. For each unvisited node, a new DFS explores its whole component. Time O(V + E), Space O(V) for visited + call stack.

examples.title: Example 2: Iterative DFS with Explicit Stack
examples.explanation: Explicit stack avoids recursion depth limits. Pop gives LIFO (depth-first). Reverse neighbor order to match recursive DFS left-to-right behavior. Time O(V + E), Space O(V).

name: BFS (Breadth First Search)
description: Explores level by level using a queue. Guaranteed to find shortest paths in unweighted graphs. Used for shortest path, minimum steps, level-order traversal, and nearest neighbor problems.

examples.title: Example 1: Shortest Path in Unweighted Graph
examples.explanation: BFS explores all nodes at distance d before distance d+1. First time target is dequeued is the shortest path. Time O(V + E), Space O(V) for visited + queue.

examples.title: Example 2: Level Order Traversal (Tree as Graph)
examples.explanation: Trees are acyclic graphs. BFS processes all nodes at current depth before children. The inner for-loop ensures we only process one level at a time. Time O(n), Space O(width).

name: Number of Islands (Grid DFS/BFS)
description: Classic grid graph problem where '1's are land and '0's are water. Count connected components of land using DFS or BFS. Demonstrates treating 2D arrays as implicit graphs.

examples.title: Example 1: DFS on 2D Grid
examples.explanation: Each '1' starts a DFS that floods the entire island, marking visited cells as '0'. Outer loop counts unvisited islands. Time O(m*n), Space O(m*n) worst-case call stack.

examples.title: Example 2: BFS Alternative (No Stack Overflow Risk)
examples.explanation: Same logic as DFS but uses a queue. Prevents call stack overflow on very large grids. Direcciones array avoids repeating boundary checks. Time O(m*n), Space O(min(m,n)).

name: Clone Graph
description: Creates a deep copy of an undirected connected graph. Tests understanding of graph traversal with a hash map to track original-to-clone node mapping, preventing infinite cycles.

examples.title: Example 1: BFS with Node Map
examples.explanation: BFS creates clone for each original node first. Then wires neighbors by looking up clones in the map. Time O(V + E), Space O(V) for the map and queue.

examples.title: Example 2: DFS Recursive Alternative
examples.explanation: DFS returns immediately if node already cloned (base case + cycle guard). Recursively clones all neighbors. Time O(V + E), Space O(V) for map + call stack.

name: Topological Sort (Course Schedule)
description: Orders nodes in a directed acyclic graph (DAG) so that for every edge u->v, u comes before v. Used for course scheduling, dependency resolution, and detecting cycles in directed graphs.

examples.title: Example 1: Kahn's Algorithm (BFS / In-Degree)
examples.explanation: Process nodes with zero in-degree first. If a cycle exists, some nodes never reach in-degree 0. Time O(V + E), Space O(V + E).

examples.title: Example 2: DFS with Cycle Detection
examples.explanation: Three-state tracking: unvisited, visiting (in stack), visited. Finding a 'visiting' node again means a cycle. Time O(V + E), Space O(V) for sets + call stack.

name: Word Ladder (Shortest Transformation)
description: Finds the shortest path between two words by changing one letter at a time. Classic BFS problem demonstrating preprocessing patterns and bidirectional BFS optimization.

examples.title: Example 1: Standard BFS with Preprocessing
examples.explanation: Generates all possible one-letter mutations (26 * word.length) per node. BFS guarantees shortest path. Time O(N * L * 26), Space O(N * L) where N=wordList size, L=word length.

examples.title: Example 2: Bidirectional BFS Optimization
examples.explanation: Expands from both begin and end simultaneously, always growing the smaller frontier. Meets in the middle faster. Cuts search space roughly in half. Time O(N * L * 26) worst case, but much faster in practice.
